In many cases, you won't write an ESLint config file from scratch, but rather, you'll use a combination of predefined and shareable configs along with your own overrides to create the config for your project. This page explains some of the patterns you can use to combine configs in your configuration file.

---
title: Configure Rules
eleventyNavigation:
    key: configure rules
    parent: configure
    title: Configure Rules
    order: 3
---

::: tip
This page explains how to configure rules using the flat config format.
:::

Rules are the core building block of ESLint. A rule validates if your code meets a certain expectation, and what to do if it does not meet that expectation. Rules can also contain additional configuration options specific to that rule.

ESLint comes with a large number of [built-in rules](../../rules/) and you can add more rules through plugins. You can modify which rules your project uses with either configuration comments or configuration files.

request.instructions: The documents are sections of the documentation of ONE open-source project at one commit. Report a conflict only when two sections make incompatible statements about the SAME option, flag, default value, limit, version requirement, or behavior, for the same product version and scope. These are NOT conflicts: values of different options; example values in code samples that merely override a default; statements explicitly scoped to an older version or to migration history; one section giving more detail than the other; different defaults that the text ties to different contexts (per-route vs global, dev vs build, agent mode vs server mode).
